title: Listening to Lead
description: How many of us go through a day without saying a word? None of us. But maybe we ought to try it. Communicating is not just about giving great speeches. It’s about allowing others to express themselves.”

blocks.markdown:
A final step to becoming an excellent communicator that Pat always emphasized is the act of listening to lead. As a leader, listening is one of the most overlooked skills you can have. But what does it really mean to listen as a leader? Is it just about nodding your head and pretending to hear what your team is saying? Absolutely not. True listening is about connecting with your team on a deeper level and attempting to understand their perspectives and needs.

How many of us go through a day without saying a word? None of us. But maybe we ought to try it. Communicating is not just about giving great speeches. It’s about allowing others to express themselves.”

Now, we know what you're thinking. I already have too much on my plate. Who has time to listen? Well, my friend, if you don't make the time to listen to your team, you're going to have a lot more on your plate in the long run. Trust us.

So, let's talk about what it means to listen as a leader. First and foremost, it means being present. That means putting down your phone, closing your laptop, and actually looking at the person speaking to you. But listening isn't just about being physically present — it's also about being mentally present. That means clearing your mind of distractions and focusing on what the person is saying. That can be tough. Sometimes, it feels like our minds are like a web browser with dozens of tabs open at once. But just like how we close some tabs to avoid a crash, we need to focus on one thing at a time to avoid a “mental crash.”

As a leader, your job isn't to have all the answers. It's to help your team find the answers themselves. That means listening to their ideas and helping them think through solutions. And if they come up with a solution that's different from what you would have done, that's OK. In fact, it might even be better. Leaders who are too afraid to listen to their teams risk stifling creativity and innovation. “Often a strong, dominant leader is the worst listener. He or she is too busy telling everyone else what to do and what to think,” Pat once noted.1

sections.body:
One-on-one conversations are a great way to get to know your employees on a personal level and understand their perspective. As your schedule allows, make it a priority to work them into your regular routine.
Here are some tips to make the most of the time in your 1:1s.

sections.title: Avoid distractions.
sections.body: Avoid distractions.

sections.title: When you're having a conversation with an employee, avoid distractions like checking your…
sections.body: When you're having a conversation with an employee, avoid distractions like checking your phone or looking at your computer. Give them your undivided attention.

sections.title: Ask open-ended questions.
sections.body: Ask open-ended questions.

sections.title: Open-ended questions can help you get a better understanding of your employee's perspecti…
sections.body: Open-ended questions can help you get a better understanding of your employee's perspective. Ask questions like, "How do you feel about this situation?" or "What do you think we can do to improve?"

sections.title: Don't interrupt.
sections.body: Don't interrupt.

sections.title: Interrupting someone when they’re speaking makes them feel like their opinions aren’t val…
sections.body: Interrupting someone when they’re speaking makes them feel like their opinions aren’t valued. Wait until they have finished speaking before responding.

sections.title: Take notes.
sections.body: Take notes.

sections.title: Taking notes during a conversation shows the other person that you’re taking their concer…
sections.body: Taking notes during a conversation shows the other person that you’re taking their concerns seriously and you value their input. It also helps you remember important details.

sections.title: Be empathetic.
sections.body: Be empathetic.

sections.title: Empathy is the ability to understand and share someone else's feelings.
sections.body: Empathy is the ability to understand and share someone else's feelings. When you're listening to an employee, try to put yourself in their shoes and understand how they are feeling.

sections.title: Repeat/confirm the issue.
sections.body: Repeat/confirm the issue.

sections.title: To show the speaker you understand the issue being communicated and to avoid any miscommu…
sections.body: To show the speaker you understand the issue being communicated and to avoid any miscommunication, listen to the employee as they share, then repeat back the problem or issue being discussed. (“Just to make sure I understand, you’re saying the problem is with the new supply chain. Is that the issue?”) This shows the employee that you’re listening and gives them a chance to clarify any additional details if needed. (“Yes, it’s mainly the supply chain, but there’s also an issue with the details on the packages out of the Denver office.”)

sections.title: Follow up.
sections.body: Follow up.

sections.title: After a conversation, follow up with your employee to let them know that you have taken t…
sections.body: After a conversation, follow up with your employee to let them know that you have taken their concerns into consideration. This helps build trust and shows that you are committed to addressing their concerns.

This helps uncover problems or feedback that may not arise solely through casual conversation.
